messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Amina, a 72-year-old widow from East Africa, came to treatment after years of trying to outrun memories of the months when her home region was caught in civil war and she was forced to remain in the area as a forester, moving through familiar woodland roads under unfamiliar danger. She described one night in particular as the turning point: she had been sheltering in a small ranger outpost when a blast erupted somewhere beyond the trees, the force of it shaking the corrugated roof and leaving everyone silent for a split second before shouting broke out. In the dark, with no clear sense of where the danger was coming from, she had felt certain that anyone nearby might be hiding something, and that uncertainty has stayed with her ever since. Now, even after years in the United States, she still notices how quickly her body tightens when people seem suspicious to her, as if she must read every glance and movement for danger before it is too late.

At first she tried to manage this fear by keeping the world loud and busy. At home she would put on the television or blast music, especially at night, because silence left her too aware of the dark corners of the room and of waking up disoriented in the middle of the night. In the apartment where she lives alone now, the switch from sleep to darkness can still bring back the same helpless alertness she felt in the war zone, and she has learned to keep a lamp on or the TV humming just to get through the hours before dawn. She also spends much of her day constantly scanning her surroundings, checking doorways, windows, and anyone lingering too long outside her building. In public she is vigilant for dangerous people, watching faces and hands, measuring whether someone is acting strangely. These habits once made her feel more in control, but over time they have begun to sharpen the very moments she fears, keeping her attention locked on signs of threat and making nighttime, sudden bangs, and people who seem off to her feel even more charged.

The result has been a narrowing of her life. Amina avoids being outdoors after dark and finds herself leaving the radio on in the house even when she would rather sit quietly and pray. When a car backfires or a heavy door slams, she flinches hard enough that her chest aches, and afterward she keeps checking the street and the hallway for movement. At work, where she still takes part-time forestry consults and visits a wooded preserve with other staff, she struggles to focus because every snapped branch or distant crack can pull her attention toward the possibility of an explosion. If a colleague pauses too long near a trailhead or speaks in a low voice with someone she does not know, she becomes guarded and watches them rather than the trees she once knew so well. She has started to say no to evening meetings and has reduced the number of places she goes alone, partly because she does not trust the dark and partly because scanning everyone and everything leaves her exhausted.

Amina is not embarrassed to admit that these patterns have become a way of life, but she is frightened by how little relief they now give her. The loud music, the television, the constant looking over her shoulder—these are the very things she reaches for when she feels unsafe, yet they keep her on edge and make the night feel longer, the dark more active, the world more full of possible attack. She is seeking help now because her sleep has become too broken and her world too small, and because she is tired of living as though every bang, every shadow, and every unfamiliar person might bring the war back into the room. What she hopes for most is to rest in the dark without fear, and what she fears most is that if she cannot, she will end up isolated in a life organized entirely around danger.
